posts.title: A simple hand-stitched leather card holder
posts.excerpt: A simple bi-fold leather card holder, stitched by hand: the full 13-step build with animated diagrams, photos of my own piece, and what I would do differently next time.
posts.content:
This is a simple card holder: a small bi-fold holder in natural veg-tan leather, stitched by hand, with two card pockets inside and Z Y stamped on the front.

Below is the guide I followed to make it: thirteen steps, a diagram for most of them (many of them animated), and photos of my own piece where I have them. The page has the animations; this is the same guide as text.

The steps are written for me, to make the piece in one go with no retries, because I was on a time crunch for my girlfriend's birthday. That is why some steps may look unnecessarily detailed.

![The finished leather card holder held in one hand, with Z Y stamped on the front and brown stitching around the edge](/blog/card-holder/finished-outside.jpg)

*Oiled and buffed: Z Y on the front, brown stitching, and a glossy edge all the way round.*

Open: 114 × 146 mm. Folded: 114 × 73 mm. Leather: 1.5 mm veg-tan. Stitching: saddle stitch.

## Before you start

> **Which side is which.** Veg-tan has a smooth *grain* side and a rough, suede-like *flesh* side. The smooth side is the outside of the finished card holder. The pockets are glued to the rough side, which becomes the inside once the body is folded in half. The Z·Y goes on the smooth side of the *front cover* half, the half that faces you when it is closed. The back cover half stays plain.

**Words used in this guide**

 
- **Smooth side (grain).** The finished side of the leather. It is the outside of the card holder.
- **Rough side (flesh).** The fuzzy, suede-like side. It faces inwards, and it is where the cement goes.
- **Offcut.** A leftover scrap of leather, used for practice.
- **Front cover and back cover.** The two halves of the body once it is folded. The front cover is the half you stamp. The back cover stays plain.
- **Fold line.** The line across the middle of the body, 73 mm from each end, where it folds in half.
- **Opening edge.** The long edge of a pocket strip that cards slide in past. It is the one edge that doesn't get cemented.
- **Tacky.** Cement that feels sticky but doesn't wet your finger or form strings. Press the pieces together at this point.
- **Groover.** The tool that cuts a line 4 mm from the edge. One light pass leaves a faint guide line. A few light passes make a shallow channel (see Recessed stitching). Neither is the same thing as the grooves in the slicker.
- **Channel (recessed stitching).** A shallow groove cut along the stitch line so the thread sits level with the surface, or just under it, instead of on top.
- **Chisel and prongs.** The punching tool for stitching holes. The number of prongs (teeth) is how many holes it makes in one hit.
- **Bevel.** Shaving the sharp square corner off an edge so it becomes a small slope.
- **Slicker.** The wooden tool with curved grooves along its sides. You rub an edge in a groove to burnish it.
- **Burnish.** Rubbing an edge hard and fast with Tokonole until friction makes it smooth and glossy.
- **Saddle stitch.** Sewing with one thread and a needle on each end, so each hole gets two passes. It holds even if one stitch breaks.
- **Backstitch.** Sewing back over a few stitches you have just made, to lock the thread.
- **Spacer.** A pencil or marker laid across the fold line, so the leather folds round it in a soft curve instead of a sharp crease.

## The pieces

| Piece | Qty | Size |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Body | 1 | 114 × 146 mm 4½ × 5¾ in |
| Pocket strip | 2 | 51 × 127 mm 2 × 5 in |

  The pocket strips are cut a little bigger than they need to be, on purpose: about 7 mm extra at the end and 6 mm on each side. You glue them on and then trim the overhang off flush in step 6. After trimming, each pocket is 44 mm deep and as wide as the body (114 mm).

 A card is 86 × 54 mm. Inside the stitch lines the body is about 106 mm wide, so cards slide in sideways with room to spare, and about 1 cm sticks out of each pocket for easy pulling. The body folds in half across the 58 mm gap between the pockets, so it closes to 114 × 73 mm.

## 1. Mark and cut the pieces

*Weaver guide · veg-tan leather · steel ruler · cutting mat · craft knife · pencil*

Three flat, square pieces: one body and two pocket strips.

1. Put the veg-tan leather on the cutting mat with the **smooth side up**. The smooth side looks finished; the other side looks fuzzy, like suede.
2. Mark the pieces in pencil using the cut list layout: body **114 × 146 mm** and two pocket strips **51 × 127 mm**.
   1. Line the steel ruler up with one straight edge of the sheet, so that edge becomes the first side of the body.
   2. Make two small pencil ticks 114 mm apart along it. Do the same 146 mm away along the sheet's other straight edge.
   3. Join the ticks with the ruler to make the body rectangle.
   4. Mark the two pocket strips the same way in the leftover leather, each 51 × 127 mm.
   5. Measure every side a second time before you cut. Within 1 mm is fine.
3. Put a fresh blade in the craft knife (the tool kit comes with 5 spare blades).
4. Cut the body first, then the two strips.
   1. Lay the ruler on the piece you are *keeping*, not on the offcut. If the knife slips it then cuts waste.
   2. Press the ruler down hard with your flat hand, with your fingers well back from its edge.
   3. Hold the knife upright, not leaning. Make a light first pass to score the line.
   4. Cut with 3 to 5 light passes in total. Don't try to cut through in one go.
5. Leave the corners square. You round them later, in step 6.
6. Check each piece against the ruler.
7. Store the pieces flat between two sheets of cardboard, out of the sun and away from damp. Keep the offcuts: you need them for practising the letters.

*Diagram: Three flat pieces of leather: one large body and two narrow pocket strips*

Three flat pieces with straight edges and square corners. Nothing is stamped, glued or finished yet.

## 2. Practise the letters, the edge and the fold

*Tandy stamping · 6 mm letter stamps · nylon mallet · sponge · stone surface · 4# beveler · Seiwa Tokonole · wooden slicker · veg-tan offcuts*

A trial run of the three things you can't undo on the real piece: stamping, finishing an edge, and folding. Use veg-tan offcuts for the letters and the fold, and two offcuts glued flat together, rough sides facing, for the edge.

### The letters

**Then do it for real:** step 3.

- Work on a **stone surface** (a granite or marble counter, or a tile). It gives crisp letters. The plastic punch board is too springy.
- **Dampen** a veg-tan offcut: wipe both sides once or twice with a well-squeezed sponge until it looks darker and feels cool, with no pooling or dripping. Wait 10 to 20 minutes, until the colour starts coming back a little.
- **Check which way up each stamp reads:** press the Z, then the Y, onto a bit of paper by hand. The mark is how the letter will appear on the leather.
- **Strike one letter:** offcut smooth side up on the stone, stamp upright (90° to the leather) and held near the top with your fingertips. Hit the top **once, firmly**, with the nylon mallet and lift it straight up. Don't rock it, and don't hit it twice.
- **Read the mark.** Blurry: the leather was too wet, so wait longer next time. Faint: it was too dry or the hit was too soft. Try again on a fresh spot.

> **Make a whole Z · Y.** Draw a pencil line across the offcut and stick masking tape with its top edge on the line. This is the baseline. Press the awl point lightly into the leather by hand to make the dot (don't hit it). Strike the Z with its centre 9 mm to the left of the dot and the Y with its centre 9 mm to the right. The bottoms of the letters sit on the tape's edge. Peel the tape off. The letters should be level, with equal gaps.

- Repeat until **three tries in a row** look clean.

*Diagram: a mallet comes down once on a letter stamp standing upright on damp leather, then the stamp lifts straight up and leaves a mark*

One firm hit, then lift straight up. The stamp stays upright (90° to the leather) so the letter is pressed in evenly. Don't rock or wiggle it, and don't hit it twice.

### The edge

**Then do it for real:** step 4, step 8 and step 11.

- **Gather:** the glued offcut strip, the 4# (0.7 mm) beveler, the Seiwa Tokonole and the nail file. Keep the beveler's cap on until you use it: the tip is very sharp.
- **Position the strip** flat on the cutting mat, with the edge you are bevelling **pointing straight away from you**. Hold it down with your other hand, fingers to the side and well clear of the edge.
- **Bevel:** set the beveler on the corner at the near end, tilted to about **45°** (step 4 has the drawings). Light pressure, and push it away from you along the whole edge in one smooth stroke. A thin ribbon of leather should curl off. Turn the strip over and bevel the other face of the same edge the same way.
- **Compare** it with the RIGHT, TOO STEEP and TOO FLAT drawings in step 4 and adjust your tilt. Try again on the other long edge.
- **Smooth the bevel** with the finer side of the nail file, held flat against the slope at the same 45° (not against the faces). Make 3 or 4 light strokes along the edge, all in the same direction, then run a fingertip along it. It should feel smooth, with no fuzz or ridges. If not, do a few more strokes.
- **Burnish:** dab a thin film of Tokonole on a 5 cm section of the edge with a fingertip. Pick the groove on the wooden slicker (from the tool kit) that fits the edge snugly, and rub quickly back and forth until it feels warm and looks glossy. Fast rubbing makes the heat. Do the next 5 cm, until the edge is finished, then do a second pass.

### The fold

**Then do it for real:** step 12.

- **Cut an offcut** about **4 cm × 15 cm** to stand in for the body, and pencil a line across the middle of its rough side. This is the fold line.
- **Dampen the fold zone:** with a well-squeezed sponge, wipe a band about 6 cm wide, centred on the fold line, on the **rough side only**. Wait about 2 minutes, until the leather looks darker and bends easily.
- **Fold it round a spacer:** lay a pencil (or a marker about 8 mm thick) across the fold line on the rough side. Bring the two ends together around it, rough sides facing in and the smooth side outside, and press gently along the fold from the middle outwards. The spacer keeps it a soft curve instead of a sharp crease. The outside of the fold should be a smooth round curve, with no cracks.
- **Clip** the two ends together with a binder clip, with folded paper under the jaws. Leave it somewhere dry and out of the sun overnight.
- **Next day,** remove the clip and the pencil. It should stay folded by itself and not spring flat.

## 3. Stamp Z·Y on the front cover

*Tandy stamping · 6 mm letter stamps · nylon mallet · masking tape · sponge · stone surface · ruler · pencil · awl*

The body folds in half across the middle, so the stamp goes on one half (the front cover), centred in that half. Centred on the whole body, the letters would sit on the fold. A stamp can't be undone, so take your time on the setup and only strike once per letter.

Key numbers: Centre 57 mm across, 36 mm up; Letters 6 mm tall; Gap 9 mm either side of the dot.

**New to this move? Practise it first:** stamping on offcuts, in step 2, part A. Get three clean Z · Y marks in a row there first.

### Set up

- **Choose the front cover.** Lay the body on the stone surface, smooth side up, with a short (114 mm) edge nearest you. With the ruler and pencil, draw a very light line across the middle, 73 mm from the near edge: the fold line. The half nearest you is the front cover. The far half is the back cover, which you leave plain.
- **Mark the centre** of the front cover: a small pencil cross **57 mm** in from the left edge and **36 mm** up from the near edge. This is where the dot goes. No letter will be closer than 12 mm to an edge or to the fold line, so at this spot they are well clear.
- **Do a dry run:** set the Z, awl and Y on the leather without hitting them, with the Z centred 9 mm left of the cross and the Y 9 mm right of it. Check the spacing, then put them down.
- **Stick the tape baseline.** The letters are 6 mm tall and centred on the cross, so their bottoms sit about 3 mm below it. Stick a strip of masking tape across the front cover with its **top edge 33 mm up from the near edge**, parallel to the near edge. Check it with the ruler, then press it on lightly.

### Stamp

- **Dampen** the smooth face of the **front cover half only**, going around the tape, with a well-squeezed sponge. It should look darker, with no pooling. Wait 10 to 20 minutes, until the colour starts coming back.
- **Dot first:** press the awl point lightly into the cross by hand.
- **Then the Z:** put its bottom on the tape's edge, 9 mm left of the dot. Stand the stamp straight up, hit it once firmly with the nylon mallet and lift it straight up. **Then the Y** the same way, 9 mm right of the dot.
- **Peel the tape off slowly.** If a letter is faint, **leave it**: hitting it again almost always makes a double image.
- **Leave the body flat overnight** to dry, away from sun and heat. Don't oil it yet.

*Diagram: the Z dot Y is stamped in order on a masking tape baseline. The card holder body is shown on the left with a fold line across the middle, a dashed stitch line and a dotted keep-clear line, and the stamp sits in the lower half, the front cover. The stamped area is enlarged on the right*

Stamp the front cover half only. The body folds in half along the dashed fold line, so the Z·Y goes in the middle of the half nearest you (57 mm across, 36 mm up), inside the dotted line. Stick tape where the bottoms of the letters will sit, stamp the dot first, then the Z on its left and the Y on its right. Letters are 6 mm tall. Schematic, not to scale.

*Diagram: The body from the front with Z dot Y stamped in the middle of the lower half, the front cover, and from the back, plain*

The Z·Y is on the front cover half , the half below the fold line. The back is untouched. The fold line is only a faint pencil mark, and it is drawn here so you can see where the fold will go.

## 4. Finish the pocket openings

*Weaver guide · 4# beveler · nail file · Seiwa Tokonole · wooden slicker*

Finish the opening edge of each pocket now, because you can't reach it once the pockets are glued on. Each strip has two long (127 mm) edges: pick one as the opening and work only on that one.

Key numbers: Angle 45°; Beveler 4# (0.7 mm); Per strip one long edge.

**New to this move? Practise it first:** bevelling and burnishing on the practice strip, in step 2, part B.

### Bevel the opening edge

- **Position a pocket strip** on the cutting mat, smooth side up, with the opening edge **pointing straight away from you** and a short end nearest you. Hold it down with your other hand, fingers well clear of the beveler's path.
- **Bevel:** set the 4# beveler on the corner at the near end, tilted to about **45°** (see the drawings below). Light pressure, and push it away from you along the whole edge in one smooth stroke. A thin ribbon should come off. Then turn the strip over and bevel the same edge on the other face.

*Diagram: End-on view of a leather edge with its top corner shaved off at 45 degrees, and the beveler tilted at 45 degrees on the corner*

End-on view, looking along the edge. You push the beveler away from you, into the page. It shaves the square corner into a small 45° slope, equal on the top face and the edge. Do the other face the same way.

*Diagram: a beveler is pushed along the edge of a leather strip, away from you, leaving a narrow bevel behind it and a thin ribbon of leather curling off ahead of it*

Top view of one pass. The strip's edge points straight away from you. The beveler sits at 45° on the corner and is pushed along in one stroke. A thin ribbon curls off, and the narrow strip left behind is the bevel.

- **Check the edge** against the RIGHT, TOO STEEP and TOO FLAT drawings. If it's wrong, practise more on the practice strip. Don't keep trying on the real piece.

*Diagram: Correct bevel: an even 45 degree slope on both faces of the edge*

Check the angle by looking at the edge end-on. A small, even slope that is the same width all along is right. If it digs in or only skims, change the tilt. The practice strip is the place to find it.

### Smooth and burnish

- **Smooth** the edge with the finer side of the nail file, held flat against the bevelled slope at the same 45°. Make 3 or 4 light strokes along the edge, all in the same direction, then run a fingertip along it: smooth, no fuzz. If not, a few more strokes.
- **Burnish** with Seiwa Tokonole and the slicker: dab a thin film on the edge with a fingertip, then rub quickly back and forth in the slicker groove that fits a single 1.5 mm layer, until it warms up and turns glossy (step 11 has a diagram). Do it a second time.
- **Do the same on the second strip.**

*Diagram: The stamped body, and two pocket strips whose opening edge, drawn in green, is bevelled and glossy*

The body is unchanged. Each pocket strip now has one long edge finished (green): that is the edge cards slide in past.

## 5. Glue the pockets on

*Fiebing's Leathercraft Cement (20 ml) · cotton buds · pencil · ruler · binder clips + paper · old cards · heavy book*

Stick each pocket onto the back of the body with the Fiebing's Leathercraft Cement (the small 20 ml bottle with no brush). It is contact cement: it grabs the moment two coated surfaces touch, so you get one go. Line everything up before they meet.

> Work near an open window, since the cement has a solvent smell. Keep the lighter away from it. Put the lid back on straight after each use, so the cement doesn't thicken.

Key numbers: Pocket depth 44 mm; Gap between 58 mm; Overhang 7 mm end, 6 mm sides; Clip 30 minutes.

### Mark the pockets

- **Put the body face down,** so its **rough back is up**. This side becomes the inside of the card holder.
- **Draw the pocket lines:** from one short end, measure **44 mm** in at both long edges, make a small tick at each and join the ticks with the ruler in a light pencil line. Do the same from the other end. Check that the two lines are **58 mm** apart. The middle of that gap, 73 mm from each end, is where the body folds later, so keep glue and clips away from it.
- **Dry fit each pocket, with no glue:** lay a strip on the body smooth side up (so its rough side is down on the body's rough side), with one long edge exactly on a pencil line. That is the opening edge, and it faces the middle. The strip should hang past the end by about 7 mm and past each side by about 6 mm, evenly. Slide a card in sideways to check it fits, pull it out, then do the other pocket. Lift both off and keep each beside its own end.
- **Mark the glue bands in pencil.** On the body: a band 5 mm wide along the end and down both sides, as far as the pencil line. On the underside of each strip: a band 12 mm wide along the end and both sides. The two bands will meet in the same place. **Keep the opening edge completely clear.** No glue goes there.

*Diagram: pencil lines are drawn 44 millimetres from each end of the body, pocket strips are dry fitted with their opening edge on the line, lifted off while glue is spread on three sides, pressed down and clipped*

Glue three sides of each pocket, never the opening. Draw the band 5 mm in from the body's edge, and 12 mm in from the strip's edge on the pocket's underside. They meet in the same place, because the overhang is trimmed off in the next step. Thin coat on both surfaces, wait until tacky, then press together.

### Glue and press

- **Spread the cement:** tip a few drops of the Fiebing's cement onto a scrap of card, pick some up with a cotton bud and spread a thin, even coat on the marked band on the body, then on the marked band on the underside of the first pocket. Both surfaces get a coat. Stay inside the pencil lines, then close the bottle.
- **Wait until it is tacky:** touch a spot lightly with a clean fingertip. It should feel sticky, but nothing should come off on your finger and it shouldn't string. A few minutes; the bottle says how long.
- **Press the pocket on:** hold it by its overhanging ends with the opening edge directly above the pencil line. Let one end touch down first, then lay the rest down like closing a book. Don't slide it around once it touches. Press hard along the glued bands with your fingers, then rub along them with the flat of the slicker.
- **Clip it:** fold a bit of paper over each clip's jaws so the metal doesn't dent the leather, and clip along the glued bands (the end and both sides), never across the opening edge or the fold zone. Leave for about 30 minutes.
- **Repeat** from the cement step for the second pocket. When both are dry, slide a card into each pocket to confirm the opening isn't stuck shut.

*Diagram: The back with two pocket strips glued on and sticking out past the body edges*

The pockets are glued to the rough back , one at each end, with their opening edges (green) facing the middle. They stick out a little past the body at the end and the sides. The 58 mm gap between them is where it will fold.

## 6. Trim flush and round the corners

*Weaver guide · craft knife · steel ruler · paper · Singapore 20-cent coin (21 mm) · pencil · nail file*

Cut off the pocket overhang so the edges are flush, round the four corners, then file everything smooth. There is a diagram for each part: the first shows the trim, the second the corners, the third the filing.

Key numbers: Trim 2 or 3 light passes; Cuts 3 per pocket, 6 in all; Corner radius about 10 mm (20-cent coin).

### Trim the overhang

- **Turn it over** so the **stamped front faces up**. The pocket overhang is now underneath, sticking out past the edges of the body. Lay a sheet of paper over the front to protect the stamping.
- **Ruler on the edge:** put the steel ruler on the paper with its edge **exactly on the edge of the body**. Look from above to check, then press it down hard with your flat hand, fingers well back from the edge.
- **Cut:** hold the knife **upright** (90° to the mat, not leaning), with the flat of the blade touching the ruler's edge, and run it down the ruler's edge in 2 or 3 **light passes**. Don't try to cut through in one go. The overhang drops away.
- **Repeat for every overhang.** Each pocket sticks out on **three sides** (its end and both of its sides), so that is 3 cuts per pocket, 6 in all. Move the ruler for each one. The long sides in the gap between the pockets have no overhang, so there is nothing to cut there.

*Diagram: the card holder lies on a cutting mat with the stamped front up, a sheet of paper over it and a steel ruler on top with its edge exactly on the body edge. A knife held upright makes three light passes down the ruler edge and the pocket overhang beyond the body falls away*

Press the ruler down, keep the blade upright, and take 2 or 3 light passes. End-on view of the card holder flipped front up, with paper over the stamping. The ruler's edge sits exactly on the body's edge, so the blade runs along the ruler and slices the pocket overhang off flush with the body. Do the end and both sides of each pocket.

### Round the corners

- **Trace the curve:** put a Singapore 20-cent coin (21 mm across) into one corner, tight against both edges, and trace its curve with the pencil. The corner radius is the coin's radius, about 10 mm. Do the same in the other three corners.
- **Cut each corner in three short straight cuts.** Make two extra pencil dots on the curve, evenly spaced, so you have four points in a row: where the curve leaves the top edge, two between, and where it leaves the side edge. Cut from point to point with the knife, using the ruler as a guide where you can, and stay on the waste side of the pencil line. Each cut takes 2 or 3 light passes, and the little piece in the corner falls away.

*Diagram: a Singapore 20 cent coin, 21 millimetres across, is traced in the corner, three short straight cuts are made along it, the waste piece falls away and the points are filed smooth*

Three short straight cuts are easier than one curve. Trace a Singapore 20-cent coin (21 mm across, so a corner radius of about 10 mm). The shaded piece is what you cut away. Do all four corners the same way, then file each one smooth.

### File smooth

- **Go all the way round all four sides** of the piece, not just where the pockets are.
- **Straight edges:** use the finer side of the file, held flat against the edge so it covers the body and the pocket layers together. Make 3 or 4 light strokes along the edge, all in the same direction, until the layers are level.
- **Corners:** use the coarser side first, filing along the curve until the three cuts blend into one round shape, then the finer side.
- **Check by touch:** run a fingertip over every edge and corner. The body and the pocket layers should feel like **one flat surface, with no step between them**. If you can feel a step or a point, do a few more strokes there.

*Diagram: on the left an end-on cross-section of the glued edge where the pocket sticks out a hair past the body, and a nail file held flat against the edge wears the step away; on the right a top view of a corner where the points left by the three cuts are filed into one round curve*

File until it feels like one piece. Use the finer side of the nail file, flat against the edge, with 3 or 4 light strokes in the same direction. On the corners, file along the curve until the three cuts blend into one round shape. Then run a fingertip over it: you should feel no step between the body and the pocket layers.

*Diagram: Both sides with rounded corners and pockets trimmed flush*

The overhang is gone, so the pockets are flush with the body, and all four corners are rounded. The front is unchanged apart from the corners.

## 7. Groove the stitch line

*Tandy saddle stitch, step 1 · adjustable groover (from the tool kit) · ruler · offcut*

Score a faint line all the way round, 4 mm in from the edge. It is your guide for the holes and keeps the stitches straight. (This is the groover's shallow line, not to be confused with the grooves in the wooden slicker.)

> Want the stitches to sit in a channel? As written, this step gives you a faint guide line, which means flat stitching. For the recessed look, make a few light passes instead of one. Recessed stitching shows how, and also how to put the groover together if it came in pieces. Decide before you cut the real piece: the cut can't be undone.

Key numbers: Groove gap 4 mm; Start middle of a short end.

### Set and test the groover

- **Set the groover:** loosen its screw, slide the guide until the gap between the guide and the blade is **4 mm** (measure it against the steel ruler), then tighten the screw.
- **Test it on an offcut:** press the guide against the offcut's edge and pull the groover along. You want a clear, shallow line, not a deep cut. If it's too faint or too deep, change the pressure.

### Score the card holder

- **Stamped front facing up.** Start in the middle of one short end. This is also where you will start punching and stitching.
- **Guide against the edge, blade on the leather, press lightly,** and pull steadily all the way round. Ease it round the corners, keeping the guide against the curve. When you get back to where you started, lift off.
- **Look along the line:** it should be continuous and the same distance from the edge everywhere.

*Diagram: an adjustable groover is pulled along the leather with one arm riding the edge while the blade scores a line 4 millimetres in*

One arm rides the edge, the other scores the line. Set the gap to 4 mm on an offcut first, keep the guide pressed against the edge and move in one steady pass.

*Diagram: The front with a dashed groove line 4 mm in from the edge*

The front has a faint groove line all the way round, 4 mm in from the edge. It is only on the front.

## 8. Bevel the outside edges

*Weaver guide · 4# beveler*

Round off the sharp outer corners, the same way as in step 4, all the way round the piece. The pocket opening edges are already done, so skip those. The edge is one layer (1.5 mm) between the pockets and two layers (3 mm) along each pocket. You bevel it the same way in both places (second diagram).

Key numbers: Angle 45°; Edge 1.5 mm between pockets, 3 mm along them.

**New to this move? Practise it first:** bevelling on the practice strip, in step 2, part B.

### Bevel the front

- **Edge by edge:** turn the card holder so the edge you are working on **points straight away from you**. Set the beveler on the corner at the near end, tilted to about **45°**, light pressure, and push it away from you along the edge in one smooth stroke.
- **Work in short sections,** joining each stroke to the last. Go round the corners in short strokes that follow the curve. Turn the piece for the next edge and repeat, until you are back where you started.

*Diagram: arrows go all the way round the edge of the front, then all the way round the back, including the pocket edges*

Front first, then flip. Use the same 45° tilt as in step 4, with the edge you're working on pointing away from you. Go round the corners in short strokes, following the curve. Arrows show one way round; the direction doesn't matter.

> **Crossing from one layer to two.** On the front you are always bevelling the body's own top corner, so the stroke doesn't change. Where a pocket's opening edge meets the side edge, the edge steps from 3 mm to 1.5 mm. Stop the stroke just before the step and lift the tool, then put it down again just past the step and carry on. Don't try to push through the step in one stroke.

### Flip and bevel the back

- The back face is the **pocket's smooth side** along each pocket, and the body's **rough side** in the gap between them. Bevel whichever one is there.
- Along a pocket you bevel the pocket's outer corner. Leave the glue seam between the body and the pocket alone. Use the same 45° tilt and the same light, single stroke, and stop and restart at the step as before.

### Blend and check

- **Blend the steps:** at each place where the edge changes from 1 layer to 2, make 2 or 3 light strokes with the finer side of the nail file to blend the two bevels.
- **Check by touch:** run a fingertip along each edge. The sharp corner should feel gone on both faces, but you should still feel a clear edge. If it digs in or only skims, compare it with the drawings in step 4.

*Diagram: End-on view of an edge with one layer of leather, with both the top and the bottom corner bevelled*

Same tool, same 45° tilt, same two strokes in both places. The 4# beveler only takes off about 0.7 mm per face, so it doesn't matter how thick the edge is. You always bevel the top corner and the bottom corner of the edge. Where there are two layers you don't bevel the glue seam between them. The burnishing in step 11 blends it in.

*Diagram: Both sides with bevelled outer edges*

Every outer edge has a small bevel (the tan line), on the front and on the back. The pocket opening edges were already done in step 4.

## 9. Punch the stitching holes

*Weaver guide · Tandy, step 2 · chisels (1, 2, 4, 6-prong) · nylon mallet · white PVC punch board*

A row of evenly spaced holes, 4 mm apart, all the way round the groove, going through both layers. The chisels have 1, 2, 4 and 6 teeth (prongs); the 6-prong does most of the work.

Key numbers: Hole spacing 4 mm; Main chisel 6-prong; Each strike one firm hit.

### Start

- **Set up:** put the card holder on the white PVC punch board, **stamped front facing up**, on a solid table. Make sure the board isn't on anything wobbly.
- **First strike:** start in the middle of one short end, the same place you started the groove. Put the 6-prong chisel's teeth in the groove, hold it straight up (not leaning) and hold the leather down with your other hand. Give it **one firm hit** with the nylon mallet, then pull the chisel straight up, wiggling it slightly if it sticks.

### Go round

- **Overlap by one hole:** put the chisel's first tooth into the last hole you made, so the spacing stays even. Hit it once and pull it straight up. Repeat until you are about to reach a corner.

*Diagram: a six-prong chisel strikes to make six holes, slides along so its first tooth sits in the last hole, then strikes again to make five more evenly spaced holes*

Overlap by one hole. Drop the first tooth of the chisel into the last hole you made (green), then strike, so the spacing carries on evenly. At corners use the 2-prong and 1-prong chisels the same way.

- **Corners:** switch to the 2-prong, then the 1-prong chisel, and punch single holes about 4 mm apart that follow the curve of the corner. Go back to the 6-prong on the next straight edge.
- **Pocket openings:** where a pocket's opening edge meets the side edge, look for a hole on each side of the opening, about 2 mm away from it. If a hole falls right on the edge, punch a 1-prong hole 2 mm to one side instead. These holes let the stitches lock the top of the pocket.

### Close the loop and check

- **Close the loop:** when you are about 20 mm from your first hole, stop and look at the gap that is left. Fill it with the 4, 2 or 1-prong chisel, whichever makes the spacing even.
- **Check the back:** every hole should be punched through **both layers** where a pocket is. If one isn't, strike a 1-prong chisel into the same hole again.

*Diagram: Both sides with a row of stitching holes all the way round*

A row of holes runs all the way round, 4 mm in, going through both layers where a pocket is. You can see them from both sides.

## 10. Saddle stitch all the way round

*Tandy saddle stitch, steps 3–8 · 2 needles + waxed thread (tool kit) · thread scissors · lighter · nylon mallet*

Sew with one length of thread and a needle on each end . Both needles go through every hole, in opposite directions, so the stitches look the same on both sides and can't unravel.

Key numbers: Thread about 2.6 m; The rule A first, B second; Backstitch 2 or 3 holes.

### Prepare the thread

- **Cut about 2.6 m** of waxed thread (the stitch line is about 50 cm round, and you need roughly 5 times that). Thread a needle onto each end and pull about 5 cm through each eye. Call one needle **A** and the other **B**.
- **Start** in the middle of one short end, at the hole where you started punching. Push needle A through the first hole, then pull the thread through until the two halves hang out of the hole, front and back, the same length.

### Stitch every hole

- **A goes first:** A is on the back, so push it through the next hole from back to front. The animation below shows each move.
- **B goes second:** B is on the front, so push it through the **same hole** from front to back. Make sure the needle goes *beside* the thread already in the hole, not through it.
- **Pull both ends snug and even.** The stitch should sit flat in the leather, not dig in or buckle it.
- **Repeat for every hole.** A always goes first and B second, through the same hole in opposite directions. After each stitch the needles have swapped sides, so at the next hole A goes from front to back and B from back to front.

*Diagram: needle A goes through hole 2 from the back to the front, then needle B goes through the same hole from the front to the back, both are pulled snug, and then the same happens at hole 3 with A going first again but this time from the front to the back*

Side view, thickness exaggerated. It is one length of thread with a needle on each end. At every hole A goes in first and B goes in second , through the same hole in the opposite direction. After each pair, pull both ends snug. The needles swap sides each time, so at the next hole A goes the other way. Each side ends up with a row of equal stitches.

> **If it goes wrong.** Every few stitches, pull the thread straight. Waxed thread tangles easily: if it does, stop and untangle it before pulling. If one stitch slants a different way from the others, you swapped the order there. Unpick it and redo it.

### Pocket openings (optional lock)

- At each pocket opening, an extra lock stitch is **optional**. The glue and the saddle stitch already hold the pocket, so you can stitch straight past.
- **To add the lock:** stitch the hole beside the opening as normal with both needles. Then take **only the needle that is on the front**, go back one hole (front to back), and come forward through the hole beside the opening again (back to front). Carry on with both needles.
- **Too tight?** Push the awl through the hole beside the thread, not through it, and wiggle gently to open the hole. If the needle still won't go, leave the lock out. Never force the needle or pull it with pliers. Don't double back with *both* needles either: that puts six threads in one hole, and they won't fit.

*Diagram: the last hole is stitched as normal, then one needle comes back one hole and goes forward again, adding one extra loop over the last two holes*

Optional: lock the pocket opening. Top view of the last holes before the opening edge, where cards pull on the stitching. Stitch hole 1 as normal with both needles. Then, with the front needle only, come back to hole 2 and go forward through hole 1 again. If it is still too tight after opening the hole with the awl, leave the lock out; never force it. Schematic, not to scale.

### Finish

- **Backstitch at the first hole:** when you reach the last hole next to where you started, sew back over the last 2 or 3 holes, as if stitching in reverse. Two holes is enough. If a hole is tight, open it first by pushing the awl through beside the thread.
- **Trim and melt:** trim both thread ends close to the leather with the thread scissors, then touch each cut end to the lighter's flame for a second, so it shrinks into a small blob. Keep the flame away from the leather and from the cement. Press the blob flat with the slicker once it cools. (No melt? Use a tiny dab of the Fiebing's cement instead.)
- **Flatten the stitches:** lay the card holder on the stone surface and tap along the stitches with the nylon mallet, working round the edge.

*Diagram: Both sides with a row of stitches all the way round*

The stitching runs all the way round and looks the same from the front and the back. The gap between the pockets is stitched along its sides too, but nothing is sewn across the middle.

## 11. Burnish the outside edges

*Weaver guide, edge slicking · nail file · Seiwa Tokonole · wooden slicker*

Turn the sanded edges into a smooth, glossy finish. Do this before oiling (oiled edges don't burnish well) and before folding.

Key numbers: Per section 5 cm; Passes 2; Slicker groove wider for 3 mm, narrower for 1.5 mm.

**New to this move? Practise it first:** burnishing the practice strip, in step 2, part B.

### Sand and burnish, first pass

- **Sand the edges smooth:** run the finer side of the nail file lightly along each outer edge. Keep the file moving so you don't wear a flat spot, and stop when the layers look and feel like a single smooth surface.
- **Dab** a thin film of Seiwa Tokonole on a 5 cm section with a fingertip.
- **Pick the groove** that fits. Where a pocket is glued on, the edge is two layers (about 3 mm), so use a wider groove. Elsewhere it is one layer (1.5 mm), so use a narrower groove.
- **Rub quickly** back and forth along the section until the edge feels warm and looks glossy. Then move on to the next 5 cm and repeat, all the way round.

*Diagram: Left: end-on view of a wooden slicker with three grooves of different sizes and a leather edge sitting in the middle one. Right: the edge before burnishing, dull and fuzzy, and after, smooth and glossy*

Rub back and forth along the edge. Wet it with a little Tokonole, then rub quickly in the groove that fits. The friction heat is what turns the sanded edge glossy. The edge is 3 mm thick where a pocket is glued on and 1.5 mm elsewhere, so use the matching groove for each.

*Diagram: Tokonole is dabbed on an edge, then a wooden slicker is rubbed quickly back and forth along it while it moves along, and the edge turns from dull to glossy behind it*

Short sections, fast rubbing. Work about 5 cm at a time. The friction heat sets the Tokonole and makes the edge shine. Rub in the groove that fits the edge, as in the drawing above.

### Second pass

- **Let the first pass dry** for a few minutes, until the edge no longer feels damp or tacky. Touch up any fuzzy spots with the finer side of the nail file.
- **Tokonole again, thinner than the first time,** and burnish each 5 cm section as before. Too much dries white.
- **Finish with cloth:** rub the edge briskly with a scrap of denim or canvas. It also reaches the rounded corners. Two passes are enough.

> **Edges still fuzzy?.** File again, use less Tokonole and rub faster. The heat from friction is what makes the shine.

*Diagram: Both sides with burnished, glossy edges*

The edges are smooth and shiny (the pale line inside the tan edge). It is still flat, with no fold yet.

## 12. Fold it and break in the pockets

*sponge · pencil or marker (8 mm) · binder clip + paper · 2–3 old cards per pocket*

Fold the body in half across the middle, with the smooth sides outside and the pockets inside, and leave it to dry in shape. The cards in the pockets loosen them at the same time.

Key numbers: Fold line 73 mm from each end; Dampen 6 cm band, 2 minutes; Clip 41 mm or wider.

**New to this move? Practise it first:** folding an offcut, in step 2, part C.

### Dampen and fold

- **Find the fold line again:** it is the middle of the 58 mm gap between the pockets, 73 mm from each end. Make a faint pencil line there on the rough side if it has rubbed off.
- **Dampen the fold zone:** with a well-squeezed sponge, wipe a band about 6 cm wide along the fold zone, on the **rough side only**. Keep it off the burnished edges, the pockets and the stamped side. Wait about 2 minutes, until the leather looks darker and bends easily.
- **Fold it round a pencil:** lay a pencil (or a marker about 8 mm thick) across the fold line on the rough side, between the pockets. Bring the two ends together around it, with the pockets facing in and the smooth sides outside, and press gently along the fold from the middle outwards. Don't force it. The outside of the fold should be a smooth round curve, with no cracks.

*Diagram: a pencil lies across the fold line on the rough side of the body. The free end is brought up and around it so the two halves lie together with the rough sides facing in and the smooth side outside, then old cards go in the pockets and a clip holds the ends together overnight*

The pencil keeps the bend round. Dampen the rough side only, lay the pencil across the fold line, bring the two ends round it and clip them. The curve around the pencil sets as it dries overnight, so the fold doesn't crack or crease. Schematic: the real leather is thinner compared with the pencil than it looks here.

### Break in the pockets

- **Slide 2 or 3 old cards** into each pocket.
- **Hold it closed** with a binder clip, with folded paper under the jaws, on the open end. It has to be a large clip (41 mm or wider): the small 15–19 mm ones don't open far enough. No large clip? Wrap the holder in plain, unprinted paper and put a rubber band round it, snug but not tight, or rest a heavy book on it.
- **Leave it overnight** somewhere dry and out of the sun.
- **Next day,** remove the clip, the cards and the pencil. It should stay folded and close nearly flat.

## 13. Oil and buff

*mink oil (30 g) · soft cloth · offcut*

Condition the leather and even out its colour. Do it after the fold has dried, because damp leather doesn't take oil.

Key numbers: Oil a pea-sized dab; Wait 30 to 60 minutes; Then overnight.

### Oil

- **Test it on an offcut first.** Mink oil darkens natural veg-tan to a warm tan, so check you like the colour.
- **Put a pea-sized dab** of mink oil on the cloth.
- **Rub a thin, even layer** over the outside, in small circles. Don't let it pool, and keep it off the burnished edges as far as you can. Then open it and do the inside and the pockets the same way.

### Buff and rest

- **Leave it 30 to 60 minutes,** then buff with a clean part of the cloth, outside and inside.
- **Leave it overnight:** the colour keeps evening out. Give it a last buff, and it is ready to wrap.

> **After oiling.** The rough side soaks up oil unevenly, so the inside can look blotchy at first. It usually evens out over a few days: don't add more oil to fix it. Don't sand a scratch once the leather is oiled, because it leaves a pale patch. Only plain, unprinted paper should touch freshly oiled leather, since it can pick up ink. Natural veg-tan darkens to a honey brown with light and handling, and it should be kept dry.

## Recessed stitching

An optional upgrade to step 7. You use the same groover and the same 4 mm distance. The difference is that you cut a shallow channel first, then punch the holes along it, so the thread sits in the channel and not on top of the leather. The leather on either side then looks slightly raised, which is the fuller look you see on many wallets.

  
### Flat (step 7 as written)

 
- Easiest, with nothing to get wrong
- Keeps the full 1.5 mm of leather
- The thread takes all the rubbing, so it wears sooner
- A plainer look

   
### Recessed (this section)

 
- The thread is protected and wears slower
- A neater, more finished look
- The channel helps keep the chisel on a straight line
- The cut can't be undone, and it takes a little strength out of thin leather

  *Diagram: Cross-section of two stitch lines. Left, flat: the thread sits on top of the leather and takes the rubbing. Right, recessed: the thread sits in a shallow channel, level with the surface, and the leather takes the rubbing.*

**Cross-section across the stitch line.** Not to scale. For recessed stitching, the channel only needs to be about as deep as the thread is thick, roughly 0.4 mm.

> **Go shallow: your leather is thin.** One experienced maker on the leatherworker.net forum says 8–9 oz leather (about 3.2–3.6 mm) is the thinnest she would cut a recessed channel in. Yours is 1.5 mm. So here the channel is shallow, about as deep as your thread is thick, roughly 0.4 mm, and never more than about a third of the leather (0.5 mm). That limit is my own cautious reading for 1.5 mm leather, not an official figure. If the offcut test makes you nervous, the faint line from step 7 is a perfectly good finish.

 
### APut the groover together

 Yours comes loose in a little bag, with a handle, a metal collar and some small parts. These are the usual steps for this style of tool. Yours may differ a little, so don't force anything. The blade is sharp: handle it by the stem and keep your fingers out of its path.

 
1. Tip everything onto the cutting mat so small parts can't roll off. The thin loose rod in the bag may be a spare blade, or a small key or screwdriver for the screws.
2. Work out which piece is which. The **blade** is the cutting piece: a thin metal tip with a sharp edge. The **guide** is the plain bent rod or bar with no sharp edge. It rests against the edge of the leather.
3. Fit the blade into the slot or hole in the stem, with the cutting tip pointing down towards the leather. Tighten its screw or collar. Give it a gentle tug: it must not move.
4. Slide the guide through the stem's cross-hole so it points the same way as the blade. Leave its screw loose for now.
5. Set the gap between the guide and the blade to **4 mm**, measured against the steel ruler, then tighten the guide's screw.
6. Give the whole tool a gentle shake. Nothing should rattle or shift. If it does, tighten the loose part.

 If the parts don't go together like this, check the seller's listing photos. The tool kit's listing has no assembly sheet that I could find.

  
### BFind the right depth on an offcut

 The blade doesn't change depth. You control it with pressure and the number of passes. Use a veg-tan offcut.

 
1. Hold the groover like a pencil. Press the guide against the offcut's edge and put the blade on the leather.
2. **First pass, light.** Pull it towards you in one smooth stroke and don't stop halfway, because stopping makes the depth uneven. You should get a faint line.
3. **Second pass** along the same line, a little firmer. The blade finds the first line by itself. Do a **third pass** only if you still don't have a clear channel. Three passes is the most.
4. Test it with thread: lay a short piece of your waxed thread in the channel. The thread should sit down in it with its top about level with the surface. If it sits on top, add one more light pass. If it disappears below the surface, it's too deep: stop and don't groove the real piece that hard.
5. If the leather looks fuzzy or torn along the line, ease off the pressure. A dull blade tears fibres instead of cutting them.

  
### CCut the channel on the real piece

 Do this in place of "press lightly" in step 7.

 
1. Put the card holder with the stamped front facing up. Start in the middle of one short end, the same place you'll start punching.
2. **Pass 1, light:** keep the guide pressed against the edge and go all the way round, easing round the corners with the guide on the curve. Lift off where you started.
3. **Pass 2** (and pass 3 if your offcut needed it): go all the way round again, along the same line, with the same pressure. Don't go deeper in just one spot.
4. Look along the line. The channel should be the same width and depth all the way round and the same distance from the edge. Turn the piece over: the back should be smooth, with no ridge or bulge.

  
### DPunch and stitch inside the channel

 
1. In step 9, put the chisel's teeth in the floor of the channel and hold it straight up. The channel keeps your row straight. The holes are still 4 mm apart.
2. In step 10, saddle stitch as normal. Pull each stitch snug so the thread sinks into the channel, but not so hard that the leather puckers.
3. The back has no channel, so its stitches sit on the surface. That's normal.

  
### EClose it over the thread

 When all the stitching is done, lay a scrap of leather over the stitch line and tap along it gently with the nylon mallet. The scrap stops the mallet from marking the leather. This is the "tap the stitches flat" in step 10. It settles the thread into the channel and nudges the channel's edges slightly over it, which gives the fuller look.

 **Done when:** the thread lies in a continuous channel, level with the surface or just under it, with the leather either side looking slightly raised. Nothing is frayed or torn, and nothing shows through on the back.

Based on [Weaver Leather: How to Use a Stitch Groover](https://www.weaverleathersupply.com/pages/how-to-use-a-stitch-groover-a-leathercraft-essential-explained) (a light, even channel; several light passes; groove before marking holes) and the [leatherworker.net thread on grooves and seam strength](https://leatherworker.net/forum/topic/7945-stitching-groovers-weaken-seam/page/2) (depth, thin leather, closing the groove over the stitches). The depth figures for 1.5 mm leather are my own cautious limit.

## If something goes wrong

- **A letter stamped faint.** Leave it. Re-striking almost never lines up exactly and makes a double image. A slightly faint letter looks handmade in a good way.
- **Stitches look uneven or slanted differently.** Always put the same needle through first and pull both threads with the same tension. Practise more on offcuts before the real piece.
- **Glue squeezed out at the edge.** Let it dry, then file it off when you sand the edges in step 11.
- **Edges stay fuzzy after burnishing.** File again, use less Tokonole, and rub faster. It's the heat from friction that makes the shine.
- **A chisel hole lands off the groove.** Keep going. Stitching hides small misses. If it's big, the next set can be angled back on line.
- **The channel came out too deep or wandered.** It can't be filled back in, which is why the offcut test comes first. A small wobble disappears once the thread is in. If it's clearly too deep, don't cut a second line: punch along the channel you have and tap the stitches flat gently.
- **The leather got a water spot.** Dampen the whole face evenly with the sponge and let it dry; the spot blends in.

## Next time

Notes from this first build, written down after burnishing. The stamp came out clean and two burnishing passes gave a glossy edge. These are the things to do differently on the next piece.

**Leather and cutting**

- **Check both sides of the leather before marking.** Look over the smooth side and the rough side for scratches, etched lines and fuzzy or thin patches, and lay the pieces out so those land in the offcuts. The rough side matters too: it is what you see inside the card holder, between the pockets.
- **Put the inner edge of the pencil line on the measurement.** A pencil line has width. Mark so the edge of the line nearest the piece sits exactly on the measurement, and cut along that edge. The whole line then ends up on the offcut, not on the piece you keep. A sharp pencil gives a thinner line.
- **Cut precisely, and don't let it drag on.** The cuts got less even the longer the cutting took. Set each cut up carefully, with the ruler checked at both ends and a fresh blade, then make it in a few steady passes. Take a short break between pieces instead of pushing on when your attention drops.

**Corners**

- **Use more, shorter cuts on each corner.** Three cuts left points that filing did not even out, so the corners came out different from each other. Mark more points along the coin's curve and make five or six short cuts, so each one takes off only a sliver and the file only has to smooth. Check each corner against the coin before moving to the next.

**Punching**

- **Use fewer prongs where there are two layers.** The 4- and 6-prong chisels would not go through the 3 mm along the pockets, and punching took a lot of time and effort. Every extra tooth needs more force. There, tap the 6-prong lightly just to mark the spacing, then punch through with the 2-prong, overlapping by one hole. Keep the 6-prong for the single layer.
- **Make each strike count.** Put the punch board on the floor or over a table leg, so nothing bounces. Give two or three firm hits with the chisel held still. Rubbing the teeth on a candle or beeswax helps them go in and pull out.
- **Finish stubborn holes with the awl.** If a hole has not gone through the back layer, push the awl (the pointed spike with a handle) through it from the front, held straight up, so it comes out in line on the back. Check that every hole is through on the back before you thread a needle.
- **Follow the curve at the corners.** Punch each corner hole by hole with the 1- or 2-prong chisel, so the stitch line follows the curve. This time it cut straight across the corners.
- **Keep the row on the line.** The stitch line wandered a little. Seat every tooth in the groove and hold the chisel upright before each strike, overlapping by one hole.

**Stitching**

- **Use thinner thread.** Small holes and thick thread made every stitch hard to pull through, and the stitches came out ropey. The kit thread is too thick for 4 mm chisel holes. Thread around 0.55 mm goes through easily, sits flatter and slants neatly. Running the awl through the holes on the two-layer parts before you start also helps.
- **Check for skipped holes as you go.** Every few stitches, and again before the final backstitch, look along both sides. Each hole should have thread in it and every stitch should be the same length. A stitch twice as long as its neighbours means a skipped hole. Unpick back to it straight away, because it is much harder to fix once the row is finished.
- **Don't double back with both needles at the pocket openings.** Three passes with two needles puts six threads in one hole, and they won't fit. Stitch straight past, or use the one-needle lock now in step 10. Open a tight hole with the awl, and never force a needle or use pliers.
- **Cover the leather when tapping the stitches flat.** A sheet of paper or a scrap of leather under the mallet stops it marking the face.

**Edges**

- **Sand the glued edges before burnishing.** After trimming, sand each two-layer edge until the layers read as one flat surface, then work through finer paper (400, 600, then 1000 grit) before any Tokonole. This is the biggest single upgrade. This time a seam line stayed visible between the body and the pockets.
- **Glue right to the edge.** Take the cement all the way out to the edge on both layers, so no gap can show in the finished edge.
- **Use less Tokonole.** A film you can barely see is enough. Thick dabs dried white in the seam and at the step where each pocket starts. Wipe any excess off straight away with a barely damp cloth, or a toothpick in the seam.
- **Second pass: let it dry, then go thinner.** Wait a few minutes after the first pass, file any fuzzy spots, then use only a trace of Tokonole. Two passes are enough; a third adds very little.
- **Finish the edges with cloth.** After the slicker, rub briskly with a scrap of denim or canvas. It evens out patchy gloss and reaches the rounded corners, where the slicker groove can't.

**The face**

- **Keep the face clean while burnishing.** Wipe your fingers before touching the face. Tokonole left a darker rim along the edges and a few faint smudges. The oil in step 13 blends them in. Don't spot-clean with water, which leaves its own mark.

**Folding and oiling**

- **Fold first, oil second.** Dampen, fold and leave it clipped overnight before any oil goes on, as in steps 12 and 13. This time the holder was only held closed after oiling, so the fold set softer and it sprang open about a centimetre. If the oil is already on, don't add water: it can spot.
- **Have a large clip ready.** The 15–19 mm binder clips were too small to go over the folded holder. Get one that is 41 mm or wider. Paper and a rubber band, or a heavy book, did the job this time.
- **Oil the rough side very lightly.** The rough side soaks up oil unevenly and the inside came out blotchy. Use only a trace there, or oil just the smooth sides.
- **Fix scratches before oiling, not after.** A scratch in the strip between the pockets could not be sanded out once the leather was oiled. Check the inside before step 13.
- **Keep a spare day at the end.** The fold needs one night and the oil needs another. Both ended up on the last night this time.

posts.title: Jellyfin stutters: Heavy processing
posts.excerpt: A follow-up to my transcoding post: Jellyfin stuttered on direct play too. The Pi's CPU was at 90%+ because qBittorrent and Bazarr were working through four seasons of a show at once.
posts.content:
In my last blog about [transcoding](/blog/jellyfin-stutter-transcoding-raspberry-pi), the stutter came down to the Pi converting a 4K Dolby Vision file it couldn't keep up with. Then it stuttered again, and this time nothing was being transcoded.

## Direct play, and still stuttering

By now I knew where to look first, so I opened the Jellyfin dashboard while it was stuttering. The session said "Direct playing". Nothing was being converted, the TV understood every part of the file and the Pi was just sending it over.

That ruled out everything from the last post. If the formats were fine and it still stuttered, then something else was keeping the Pi from sending the file fast enough.

## Look at the CPU

So I SSHed into the Pi and looked at what it was doing. The CPU usage was sitting at 90% or more, which is a lot for a Pi that is supposed to be just playing a file. If your stack runs in Docker, this shows which container is busy:

```bash
docker stats --no-stream
```

What I checked, in order:

- **Jellyfin session:** "Direct playing", so nothing was being converted. Ruled out.
- **CPU usage over SSH:** 90%+ busy, so the Pi was overloaded. The problem.
- **The busy apps:** Bazarr and qBittorrent, working through four seasons of Tulsa King at once. The cause.

## Who was using it

After digging around, it was Bazarr and qBittorrent. Seerr had been instructed to request a show with four seasons, Tulsa King, and had all of it queued up, and both of them were churning through all of it at once.

Seerr hadn't done anything wrong. The person who requested the show wanted all the seasons, so it asked for all four.

Everything in the stack lives on the same Pi, with the same four cores. qBittorrent is busy for as long as it has many active torrents, and Bazarr is busy for as long as it has a pile of episodes to look at. Jellyfin only needed a small share to direct play one file, but when two apps take most of the CPU, that share gets squeezed.

## The fix: one torrent at a time

I limited qBittorrent to one active torrent. The rest of the season now waits in the queue and gets worked on one after another, so there is much less going on at any moment. While playing a movie or show, the CPU is back to around 20 to 30%, and the stutter is gone.

In qBittorrent this is in the options, under BitTorrent and then Torrent Queueing. Set the maximum active torrents to 1. The labels might differ a little on your version.

It does mean a whole show takes longer to arrive, since the episodes are no longer downloading side by side.

## Watching it without SSH

This is the second time a stutter turned out to be the Pi working too hard, so a graph is easier than SSHing in every time. Beszel, the monitoring dashboard from the [last post](/blog/jellyfin-stutter-transcoding-raspberry-pi), shows the CPU chart too. Picking 12 or 24 hours shows what happened last night.

posts.title: Jellyfin stutters: Transcoding
posts.excerpt: A follow-up to my arr stack post: how Jellyfin chooses between direct play and transcoding, why one TV stuttered on a 4K Dolby Vision film, and why the Raspberry Pi struggles.
posts.content:
At the end of my [arr stack post](/blog/raspberry-pi-media-server) I wrote that the TVs "can stream pretty smoothly most of the time" and that transcoding was outside the scope of the blog. This is the blog about the transcoding part, now that I've had the setup running for a few weeks.

I would say that transcoding is one of the biggest pain points of running the arr stack on a Raspberry Pi instead of a mini PC. To sum up transcoding: a video file is a bundle of a video format, one or more audio formats, and a container around them. A TV can only play the formats its hardware and app understand, and older TVs understand fewer of them. Jellyfin handles that in one of three ways:

The Pi struggles with video because it has no hardware video encoder, so the work lands on its CPU. Many mini PCs can hand this job to their graphics hardware, such as Intel's Quick Sync, so the same transcode barely registers.

This one is more of a notes post than a tutorial.

## The stutter

One night my parents put on *Fury* on the TV and it stuttered badly. Not a dropped frame here and there, but stop-start playback, as if the network was lagging. There were a few guesses as to why that was happening, for example the Ethernet being too slow for the 4K movie that was being streamed, transcoding, and so on, but it was only one movie, so I shrugged and moved on.

The next night *The Departed* did the same thing. The movie was borderline unwatchable, so I went looking.

## Look at the session, not the device

Jellyfin's dashboard shows every live session (Profile → Dashboard), and for each one it tells you whether it is "Direct playing" or transcoding, and why. Open it while the stutter is happening and the reason is usually right there in the live session information.

Here is what it showed for the TV (running the Jellyfin Android TV app 0.20.0):

- **Video:** 4K, Dolby Vision. Re-encoded, at about 12 frames per second, which is half of real time, so it stutters.
- **Audio:** Italian and English tracks, both Dolby Digital (AC3) 5.1. Converted to AAC, because the TV's app told Jellyfin it can't play AC3.

## Why one TV converts what another plays

The TV, or really the Jellyfin app running on it, tells Jellyfin which formats it can decode. Jellyfin checks every part of the file against that list. Whatever is on the list plays as it is, and whatever is missing gets converted. That is why the same file can direct play on one TV and transcode on another. The file doesn't change, the list does.

A file has several things in it: the container around everything, the video, the HDR on top of it, the audio and any subtitles. Each comes in several formats, and the TV has to understand each one it meets. Rough guide to how likely a TV is to play each without conversion:

- **Container:** MP4 is the most widely supported. MKV is used by most releases, and a TV that doesn't like it but is fine with what's inside only needs a direct stream, which is cheap.
- **Video:** H.264 (AVC) plays almost everywhere and is used by most 1080p releases. HEVC (H.265) plays on most modern TVs and is used by nearly every 4K release. AV1 only plays on recent devices and is still rare in releases.
- **HDR:** HDR10 is understood by most 4K TVs. Dolby Vision needs a TV and app that support it, otherwise the picture may have to be converted.
- **Audio:** AAC plays almost everywhere. AC3 (Dolby Digital) and E-AC3 (Dolby Digital Plus) play on most modern TVs, depending on the app and its settings. DTS is often missing on TVs. TrueHD and DTS-HD MA (lossless Blu-ray and 4K audio) usually need a soundbar or receiver.
- **Subtitles:** text ones such as SRT are drawn by the app, so there is nothing to convert. Image-based ones such as PGS (from Blu-rays) can force Jellyfin to burn them into the picture, which means re-encoding the video.

Which formats a TV can play depends on its chip and on the app running on it, so treat this as a rough guide. Dolby and DTS formats need licences, which is part of why cheaper and older TVs skip some of them.

So the cheap, easy combination is H.264 video with AAC audio, because nearly everything plays it. The risky one is the opposite end: Dolby Vision video with a Dolby or DTS audio track. Any one of those can be the thing a particular TV doesn't understand.

## What Radarr and Sonarr will actually download

Radarr (movies) and Sonarr (TV) know nothing about your TVs. They pick a release using the quality profile you give them, and a quality profile is mostly about resolution and source (for example 1080p Blu-ray or 2160p WEB-DL), with a size range. It says nothing about the video codec or the audio.

Custom formats are where you can be pickier. A custom format matches words in the release name, like x265, DV, Atmos or TrueHD, and gives it a score. Give a format a positive score to prefer it, or a negative one to avoid it. Without any, a 4K profile will happily grab whichever release ranks best for that quality, Dolby Vision and Dolby audio included. That is how a file like this one ended up on the Pi. Radarr and Sonarr also never convert anything. They download the release as it is.

The tags in a release name are what you can match on. Two made-up examples, taken apart:

- `2160p WEB-DL DV HDR DD5.1 H.265`: 4K, from a streaming service, Dolby Vision, HDR10, AC3 audio, HEVC video. Plays fine on a TV that handles Dolby Vision and Dolby audio. Otherwise the Pi has to convert it.
- `1080p WEB-DL AAC2.0 H.264`: Full HD, from a streaming service, AAC stereo, AVC video. Both formats are understood almost everywhere, so there is nothing for the Pi to convert.

## The audio was cheap, the video wasn't

Converting audio on its own is cheap, even for a Pi. If AC3 to AAC was the only thing happening, I'd never have noticed.

The expensive part was the video. The session showed the picture being re-encoded as well, and the Raspberry Pi 5 has no hardware video encoder, so that happens in software on the CPU. The CPU can only manage 12 frames per second, which is half of real time.

Converting AC3 doesn't normally force a video re-encode, so the picture was probably being converted for its own reason, most likely the Dolby Vision or HDR handling. The dashboard lists the transcoding reason for each stream, so that is the place to confirm it. Either way, this is what happened to this file:

1. Audio: the TV can't play AC3, so the audio is converted to AAC. This is cheap, and the Pi copes.
2. Video: the 4K Dolby Vision picture is re-encoded on the CPU, only 12 fps, half of real time, so it falls behind.
3. Playback stutters.

That also explains why my other TV was fine. It direct-played *No Time to Die* because that file's audio is AAC, so there was nothing to convert.

## The fix: get the TV to accept AC3

If the TV plays AC3 as it is, nothing gets converted and the Pi never has to touch the video. All of this is in the TV's Jellyfin app, under Settings → Playback. Change one setting at a time and check the dashboard in between:

1. **Audio output:** set it to "Direct", not "Downmix to stereo". In downmix mode the app only accepts AAC, MP2 and MP3, so every Dolby file gets converted.
2. **Bitstream Dolby Digital audio:** turn it on, only if the TV or its soundbar handles Dolby Digital.
3. **Prefer FFmpeg for audio playback:** turn it on if it still converts after the first two, so the app decodes the audio itself.
4. **Then check:** play something for a minute. You want to see "Direct playing" in the session.

## The fallback: stop downloading Dolby Vision

If none of those settings work, then that TV can't play Dolby audio through this app, and I can't fix that from the Pi.

What I can do is change what comes in. In my case, the Dolby Vision release is the one where the video got re-encoded as well, so the fallback is to tell Radarr to avoid them. A 4K HDR10 or a 1080p release with the same audio would at worst cost the Pi an audio conversion.

## On the other hand, a TV streamer is coming

The house is getting a TV streamer, and the hope is that it takes some of the transcoding off the Pi and lets us play more video formats. That is mostly true, but not quite the way I first pictured it.

A streamer doesn't transcode anything on the Pi's behalf. What it does is run the Jellyfin app on better hardware, with a decoder that understands more formats (HEVC, Dolby Vision, Dolby Digital and so on) and usually the licences for them. When the app tells Jellyfin "I can play that", Jellyfin direct plays and the Pi just sends the file. So the conversion doesn't move to the streamer, it stops being needed.

There are catches. Streamers differ a lot, so check the specs for the formats from the guide above (HEVC, Dolby Vision, Dolby Digital and Digital Plus) before buying. The TV and soundbar still matter, since the streamer can decode Dolby Vision but the TV has to be able to show it, and lossless audio like TrueHD needs a soundbar or receiver to handle it. And whatever the streamer still can't play will still land on the Pi.

## A graph I can look at without opening a terminal

While I was at it, I wanted something nicer than SSH to see what the Pi was doing. I set up Beszel, a lightweight monitoring dashboard, and it showed the Pi straight away. It's at port 8090 on the Pi.

For "what happened last night", I pick 12 or 24 hours and look at the CPU and the disk charts.

Beszel can also send alerts when a threshold is crossed, but it needs a notification method such as email set up first, which I haven't done yet.

posts.title: Jellyfin: Avoiding subscriptions like the plague
posts.excerpt: How I set up an arr stack (Jellyfin, Radarr, Sonarr, Prowlarr and qBittorrent) with Docker Compose on a Raspberry Pi 5 8GB and a 1TB external hard drive.
posts.content:
A few weeks ago, I got tired of constantly asking my girlfriend to bring her iPad over to my house just to watch shows and movies. I have a TV at home, and constantly using the iPad never felt right.

I've never had a Netflix subscription, because I never knew if I could make it worth it. Would I really watch at least $20 of shows every month?

Then I stumbled onto some YouTube Shorts about setting up an *arr stack (Radarr, Sonarr, Jellyfin and friends), and it piqued my interest. It didn't look difficult or complicated, and it sounded like a fun weekend project.

This post is how I set it up, in the order that worked for me, with bits you can click on as you read.

## What I'm actually building

One Raspberry Pi runs all of the software, and the movies and series sit on an external hard drive. An arr stack is a set of self-hosted apps, most of them named Something-arr, that find, download and organise movies and TV shows for a media server. Nine pieces fit together here: Jellyfin (the media player), Seerr (the request website), qBittorrent (downloads the files), Radarr (movies), Sonarr (TV shows), Prowlarr (indexers), Bazarr (subtitles), FlareSolverr (gets Prowlarr past anti-bot checks) and Maintainerr (auto-deletes old media).

## Why isn't this just one plug-and-play app?

Nine containers is a lot of moving parts for "watch a movie". It makes sense when you think about it: each app does exactly one job, and they talk to each other through plain web addresses and API keys.

The upside is the flexibility to swap, update or switch off any single piece without touching the rest. You will feel the downside while setting everything up, though: more things to set up and keep updated. Debugging can also be a hassle.

## Picking the Pi, and everything else I needed

I went with the Raspberry Pi 5 8GB. The whole shopping list came to S$314.31, using a spare 1TB external hard drive I already had. It took about a week for everything to arrive, since some of the parts came from London.

## Setting it up, step by step

The core components are quite linear: flash the Pi, install Docker, mount the drive, launch the stack, then connect qBittorrent, Radarr, Sonarr, Prowlarr and Jellyfin. The optional apps (Seerr, Bazarr, FlareSolverr and Maintainerr) come in any time.

## My compose file, with your pick of containers

This is my stack written as a docker-compose file, with a builder that checks whether each container has what it depends on.

## Why every app mounts the same /data

Radarr and Sonarr don't copy a finished download into the library, they hardlink it: one file on disk, two names. That only works if both names live on the same mount.

## Getting the apps to talk to each other

Every connection screen asks for a host. The containers all share one Docker network, so the most reliable way is to use the container name. A reserved IP address for the Pi works as well.

## Things that usually go wrong

Nearly every problem I had comes down to a wrong address, a wrong path or a missing permission.

## Day to day

Day to day it's just: open Seerr, request something, wait. All of the TVs have the Jellyfin TV app installed, and can stream pretty smoothly most of the time. Transcoding is the exception, and I cover it in [Jellyfin stutters: Transcoding](/blog/jellyfin-stutter-transcoding-raspberry-pi). Pretty good convenience overall, and I think it's pretty worth it.

I only use this for content I'm legally entitled to download.

posts.title: Render Error: Cannot read property 'createClient' of null
posts.excerpt: Faced some issues tinkering with React Native's BLE library and trying to get it to work.
posts.content:
Faced some issues tinkering with React Native's BLE library and trying to get it to work. Was following this [repo](https://github.com/friyiajr/BLESampleExpo) and was faced with `Render Error: Cannot read property 'createClient' of null` while trying to load the app on Expo Go.

The app seems to be crashing on the line: `new BleManager()`, but loading the app on emulator works fine and crashes on Expo Go. Weird!

## Development Server

1) After playing around I finally got `BleManager()` to stop crashing after setting up the project to use a development build by running 

```bash
expo prebuild
```

2) Create a development build like so:

```bash
npx eas build --profile development
```

3) Scan the QR, install the app on your phone and open it. Then you will need to run the dev server for your development build:

```bash
yarn start --dev-client
```

The server should appear on the development build on your phone and then you can run your mobile app.

posts.title: How to contribute to Padawan Wallet
posts.excerpt: A quick summary of what the Padawan Wallet is, why it exists and how you can contribute to it!
posts.content:
A quick summary of what the [`Padawan Wallet`](https://github.com/thunderbiscuit/padawan-wallet) is, why it exists and how you can contribute to it!

## `Padawan Wallet`

The `Padawan Wallet` project started as a passion project by [@thunderbiscuit](https://github.com/thunderbiscuit) to play around with the newly created `BDK-Kotlin` library.
He envisioned a small android app that users can use to learn about bitcoin wallets.
Users will download the wallet, go through its tutorials and delete the app with full confidence that they can navigate other bitcoin wallets on the market. 

With the power of android, `BDK-Kotlin` and the bitcoin testnet network he created the first version of the `Padawan Wallet` as an open-source project.
After `Summer of Bitcoin` came around thunderbiscuit signed up as a mentor and brought in students to not only learn about bitcoin but to contribute to the project. 

The reason why this blog post exists is also because I worked on the project as part of my `Summer of Bitcoin` internship too. 
I brought the project from using fragments to Jetpack compose alongside the help many designers.

## How to contribute

As of writing this post the current `Padawan Wallet` project is undergoing a major shift to using the `Summer of bitcoin`
If you do want to help out or just check out the project codebase feel free to join the [discord server](https://discord.com/invite/hbMszDMP3X) where we all are!
You can drop thunderbiscuit or me and message on any questions you have about the codebase and we will be more than happy to reply.

The project uses Jetpack Compose to create the UI, and you can take a look at the design wireframe on our discord.
There are many open issues on the github, most of which are outdated and will be cleared once the project is moved to the Compose framework.

Of course, you can also use the project as inspiration on how to use the `BDK-Kotlin` library. 
The library is written in Rust, so do take a look if you are interested, it is also an open-source project!

Lastly, I just want to thank thunderbiscuit for teaching me about the bitcoin network and how to navigate the project codebase throughout the 3 months.
